claim: When a jailbreak attack succeeds against a safety-aligned LLM, the model's safety-relevant internal representations are not eliminated — they are bypassed. The attack selectively suppresses a small subset of attention heads, and suppressing that subset is by itself enough to turn a refusal into a compliance, while other heads go on representing the harmful content even as the attack succeeds. Because those representations persist, they can be read out directly as a harmful-input detector, with no additional training, at a quality competitive with dedicated safety models.
experiments_evaluated: To address subclaims 1, 2, 3, 4, and 6, run an observational activation/attention study on an open safety-aligned model such as Llama-2-7B-Chat, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, or Mistral-7B-Instruct using public harmful/benign and jailbreak datasets such as HarmBench, AdvBench, and JailbreakBench. For each harmful request, create three conditions: plain harmful prompt, successful jailbreak-wrapped harmful prompt, and semantically matched benign prompt. Record per-layer/per-head attention outputs, attention weights, residual-stream activations, and final refusal/compliance behavior. First identify successful jailbreak cases by automatic refusal/compliance classification plus human spot checks. Then compare whether harmful-content information remains decodable or separable in head outputs/residual activations during successful jailbreaks, while also measuring which heads show large activation/attention-output reductions relative to the plain harmful-refusal condition. If harmful-vs-benign information remains strong in many activations during successful jailbreaks but a small set of heads is consistently suppressed, this supports the “bypassed rather than eliminated” account. If harmful information largely disappears throughout the network, it supports elimination. If no small, consistent suppressed head subset exists, it weakens the selective-suppression subclaim. This experiment could be made partly unnecessary by existing released activation traces and head-level analyses on the same models and jailbreak datasets.

To address subclaim 5, perform causal head-intervention experiments using the small suppressed head subset identified in Experiment 1. On plain harmful prompts that the model normally refuses, ablate or downscale only those heads’ outputs at the relevant layers during inference, then measure whether the model shifts from refusal to compliance; include controls that ablate random same-sized head subsets, heads with similar activation magnitude but not jailbreak-suppressed, and all heads outside the candidate subset. Conversely, on jailbreak prompts that normally succeed, restore or patch the candidate heads’ activations from the corresponding plain harmful-refusal run and test whether refusals return. If ablating the candidate subset alone reliably turns refusals into compliance and restoring it reverses jailbreak success, while controls do not, this strongly supports the causal bypass claim. If ablation has little effect or many unrelated head subsets produce the same effect, the claim that this particular small subset is sufficient is weakened. This experiment may be unnecessary if prior work already provides causal activation-patching or head-ablation evidence for the exact model, attack set, and head subset.

To address subclaims 7, 8, and 9, evaluate whether the persistent representations can serve as a no-training harmful-input detector competitive with dedicated safety models. Using held-out public datasets such as HarmBench, BeaverTails, ToxicChat, OpenAI Moderation-style public replicas, and JailbreakBench, define a detector directly from the internal signals found in Experiment 1 without fitting classifier weights—for example, a fixed aggregation of harmful-content activation scores from the persistent heads/layers, with at most a threshold chosen on a small validation split and then frozen. Test on clean harmful prompts, benign prompts, and successful jailbreak prompts, and compare AUROC, AUPRC, F1 at fixed false-positive rates, and jailbreak-detection recall against dedicated public safety classifiers such as Llama Guard, ShieldGemma, or Detoxify. If the direct readout detects harmful intent in successful jailbreaks and approaches dedicated-model performance, it supports the detector claims. If it requires trained probes to work, fails on jailbreaks, or performs far below dedicated safety models, it weakens the “no additional training” and “competitive” subclaims. This experiment could be made unnecessary by a public benchmark showing frozen internal-representation readouts evaluated against the same safety baselines on the same held-out datasets.
reference_experiments: Before identifying any component, test the premise that attacks bypass rather than erase safety representations. On inputs where a jailbreak succeeded, measure activation of the refusal direction across all layers and components (attention heads and MLPs) and compare against the same requests unattacked. If a successful attack flattens refusal activation everywhere, attacks do break safety representations and everything downstream is dead. The authors find mid layers still maintain substantial refusal activation under successful attack, particularly in the layers previously identified as most safety-relevant.

Construct the paired evaluation set the whole analysis depends on. Sample benign prompts from Alpaca, collect harmful behaviours from published harmful-behaviour datasets, generate attack variants with GCG, AutoDAN, many-shot jailbreaking and PAIR, and retain only pairs where the unattacked request is refused and the attacked version succeeds. Within-pair comparison is what separates the attack's effect from differences between requests. The authors obtain 378 (Llama-2-7B-Chat) and 176 (Llama-3-8B-Instruct) usable pairs from roughly 10,000 attack samples, a 2-3% yield that caps the study's statistical power.

Build and calibrate the component-scoring instrument. Extract the refusal direction by difference-in-means and select the optimal layer, project it into each attention head's output space to score that head's contribution to the refusal signal, and classify heads by distribution overlap between conditions using two-stage filtering. Then verify the classification is not an artifact of the cut point by sweeping the threshold and the KDE bandwidth. The authors use thresholds of 0.5, find stability across 0.4-0.6, and obtain 21 ACHs and 17 SAHs for Llama-3 (416 heads analysed) and 20 ACHs and 19 SAHs for Llama-2 (480 analysed), with ACHs concentrated in layers 0-3 and SAHs in layers 5-12.

Test causally whether suppressing the identified heads is sufficient to cause attack success. On harmful inputs the model normally refuses (baseline ASR about 0%), inject a negative refusal-direction feature into ACH outputs, progressively increase the number of intervened heads, and measure attack success rate — with a matched random-head intervention as control, 10 seeds and 95% confidence intervals. Without the random-head arm the effect cannot be attributed to those heads rather than to perturbing that many heads at all. The authors report ACH intervention driving ASR to 99.5% (Llama-3) and 83.7% (Llama-2), reaching 95.0% and 81.6% at just 8 heads, against 4.0% +/- 3.7 and 10.2% +/- 11.6 for random heads.

Test whether the other head type is a real source of the persistent signal. Apply the same suppression to SAHs, this time on attack inputs, and measure the change in mid-layer activation strength using mean absolute activation across mid-layer heads. The authors report Llama-2 falling from 0.222 to 0.181 (18%) and Llama-3 from 0.0062 to 0.0053 (14%), against a reference of 0.397 and 0.0086 under unattacked harmful inputs.

Discriminate the mechanistic account from the rival explanation that the two head types simply differ in sensitivity to harmful content. Using the linearity of attention, attribute each head's activation to individual input tokens, separate the contribution of the original harmful-request tokens from that of the attack-template tokens, and compare the two head types on each. The account holds only if the types are indistinguishable on the harmful request itself and separate sharply on the attack template. The authors report medians within +/-0.15 on harmful tokens, against roughly -1.5 for ACHs and +1.5 for SAHs on attack-template tokens.

Validate externally that the persistent signal generalises and is useful. Build a training-free detector that reads standardised activations at discriminative positions via top-m aggregation and thresholds the score, then evaluate Macro-F1 on ten safety-eval benchmarks across six models from three architecture families, against both the model's own refusal behaviour and trained guard models. If the readout does not transfer, the phenomenon is a property of the two models analysed. The authors report Gemma-2B improving from 0.470 to 0.853 and Qwen-7B from 0.506 to 0.860 overall, SALAD-Bench from 0.270 to 0.976, and Llama-3-8B reaching 0.888 weighted average against WildGuard 0.880 and LlamaGuard3/4 at 0.599/0.666.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A paired, layer- and component-resolved comparison of safety-relevant internal signals in successful attacks versus the corresponding unattacked refusals, capable of distinguishing persistence from network-wide erasure.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed experiment 0 creates plain and successful-jailbreak conditions for the same harmful requests and examines head outputs and residual activations throughout the network. Its explicit persistence-versus-disappearance comparison would reveal whether safety-relevant harmful information remains during successful attacks.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A controlled evaluation set containing within-request pairs in which the original is refused and the attacked version succeeds, so the attack effect is not confounded with changing the underlying request.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A reproducible component-level procedure that identifies the selectively suppressed head subset and distinguishes it from heads retaining the safety-relevant signal, with enough calibration to make the classification interpretable rather than an arbitrary cut.
reference_coverage.rationale: Experiment 0 provides a head-level screen for activation or output reductions and searches for a small consistent suppressed subset; experiment 1 then tests that candidate subset causally and includes several controls. However, the set does not specify a refusal-direction contribution score, an explicit classification of the complementary persistent-head population, or threshold/bandwidth sensitivity checks. The team could identify a candidate subset, but its boundary and distinction from heads that merely have different activation magnitudes would remain less well established.
reasoning_chain: [1] Reference experiment 2 establishes a calibrated way to identify and distinguish the two relevant head populations, rather than relying only on an informal notion of a large reduction.
[2] Proposed experiment 0 searches for heads with large reductions and consistency, while proposed experiment 1 tests the resulting candidate causally.
[3] Neither proposed experiment specifies the reference’s refusal-signal contribution measurement or robustness of the head-class boundary across scoring choices.
[4] Therefore the proposed set gets at component selectivity but leaves the classification and its stability ambiguous.
[5] A team running this set would fail to learn a comparably calibrated, robust separation of suppressed versus persistent head types: partial.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A causal intervention showing that suppressing the particular small candidate subset changes normally refused harmful inputs to compliance, with matched perturbation controls that rule out a generic effect of modifying the same number of heads.

But those controls are described on plain harmful prompts with refusal/compliance as the outcome; the set does not explicitly suppress the persistent heads on successful attack inputs and measure the mid-layer activation signal itself. Consequently it can suggest that other heads matter, but cannot cleanly establish that they are the causal source of the persistent signal under attack.
reasoning_chain: [1] Reference experiment 4 tests whether the persistent signal is actually supplied by the non-suppressed head population by suppressing that population on attack inputs and measuring the internal signal.

[2] Proposed experiment 0 establishes observational persistence, and proposed experiment 1 perturbs some non-candidate heads, but its stated condition is normally refused plain harmful prompts and its stated outcome is behavior.
[3] A behavioral effect or lack of effect under that different condition does not identify whether the persistent attacked-state activation itself comes from those heads.
[4] The team would therefore not obtain an unambiguous causal attribution of the persistent signal to the other head type: partial.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A token-resolved attribution that separates original harmful-request content from jailbreak-template content, allowing the head-type difference to be tested against the rival explanation of general harmful-content sensitivity.
reference_coverage.rationale: None of the proposed experiments decomposes each head's activation by token source or compares the two head populations separately on original harmful tokens versus attack-template tokens. Head-level reductions and harmful-versus-benign decoding cannot distinguish template-driven suppression from a general difference in sensitivity to harmful content.
reasoning_chain: [1] Reference experiment 5 discriminates the selective-template mechanism from the rival account that the head types simply differ in harmful-content sensitivity.
[2] Proposed experiment 0 compares whole prompts and head activations but contains no token-level attribution or source-specific decomposition.
[3] Proposed experiments 1 and 2 intervene on heads or aggregate their signals, which also cannot identify which input-token group caused the difference.
[4] The team would fail to learn whether the mechanistic separation is specific to attack-template tokens rather than intrinsic harmful-content sensitivity: missing.

evidence.quote: Token-level attribution further shows that ACH suppression is driven specifically by attack-template tokens
evidence.bearing: This is the token-source discrimination absent from the proposed set.

reference_coverage.adequacy: An externally held-out, training-free readout of persistent internal signals evaluated on both ordinary and adversarial harmful-input detection, across multiple models and diverse evaluation sets, with direct comparison to dedicated safety systems.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed experiment 2 does test a frozen no-training aggregation on clean, benign, and successful-jailbreak inputs, uses several public datasets, reports multiple detection metrics, and compares against dedicated safety classifiers. However, it does not commit to evaluation across multiple target models or architecture families, and it gives no pre-specified operational criterion for 'competitive.' Thus it would establish usefulness for the selected setting but leave transfer and comparative competitiveness materially ambiguous.
reasoning_chain: [1] Reference experiment 6 establishes both practical detector utility and external transfer by testing ordinary and adversarial settings across many datasets and model families against safety-model baselines.
[2] Proposed experiment 2 covers the no-training readout, adversarial detection, held-out data, and baseline comparison.
[3] But the proposed set names datasets and baselines without requiring several target architectures or a cross-model evaluation, and 'approaches' dedicated-model performance is not a decision rule.
[4] The team would learn whether the readout works in its chosen setting, but not whether the result transfers broadly or is demonstrably competitive under a defined standard: partial.

evidence.quote: simply reading these persistent activations—without any training—yields competitive aggregate detection performance
evidence.bearing: Confirms that the reference property is a training-free, performance-validated readout, which proposed experiment 2 addresses in part.

evidence.quote: We evaluate detection performance under the safety-eval framework ... covering 10 datasets in two scenarios: general intent recognition and adversarial-attack detection.
evidence.bearing: Confirms the breadth and dual ordinary/adversarial scope that is only partially specified in proposed experiment 2.

runs.sufficiency_reasoning: The proposed set would provide substantial evidence for persistence, localized suppression, causal sufficiency of the candidate subset, and the feasibility of a training-free detector. It would not, however, settle the full mechanistic claim as written with comparable evidential force: the persistent head population is not causally tested as the source of the attacked-state signal, the token-level rival explanation is not addressed at all, and external detector competitiveness is not committed across a sufficiently broad model scope with a defined comparison rule. The missing token-source experiment is especially important for distinguishing the claimed selective bypass mechanism from a less specific harmful-content-sensitivity account.
missing: Perform token-level attribution/decomposition separating original harmful-request tokens from attack-template tokens for the two head populations.
On successful jailbreak inputs, suppress the persistent/non-compromised heads and directly measure the resulting mid-layer safety activation, with suitable controls.
Define and validate a reproducible head-scoring/classification rule with sensitivity analysis, and evaluate it across multiple target architectures.
Pre-specify what performance margin or statistical criterion counts as competitive with dedicated safety models.
